checks.title: Linearity in the logit

verdict.text: No continuous predictor is non-linear (smallest p = 0.022, for Diastolic BP).

checks.detail: Each continuous predictor was tested with a Box-Tidwell term. The threshold is 0.05 divided by the 8 tests, which is 0.0063. 1 more fall between that and 0.05: Diastolic BP. Cigarettes per day contains zeros, so 1 was added before taking logarithms.

checks.title: Influential observations

verdict.text: No row is highly influential (largest Cook's distance 0.012).

checks.detail: 388 of 4,240 rows exceed the common 4/n guideline (0.00094), which is expected in a large sample. The largest Cook's distance is 0.012; values above 1 would be a concern. No row was removed.

verdict.text: 2 of 4 sensitivity checks changed something. See below.
Allowing a curve for Diastolic BP improves the fit only slightly (AIC better by 3.2, p = 0.028), and no other odds ratio moves by more than 2.9%. The straight-line version is reasonable.
Allowing a curve for Age improves the fit only slightly (AIC better by 0.9, p = 0.086), and no other odds ratio moves by more than 2.1%. The straight-line version is reasonable.

Using only the 3,658 complete rows changes whether there is clear evidence for Prior stroke and Total cholesterol, and moves the odds ratio for Prior stroke by 23%. The way gaps were filled matters for these results.
Removing the 42 most influential rows moves the odds ratio for Diabetes by 48%. That estimate rests on a few rows, so read it with caution. This is only a check: no row was removed from the model.

Modest discrimination. On the unseen test rows the model scores AUC 0.70 (5-fold cross-validation 0.73, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.78). At the chosen cut-off of 0.15 it catches 60% of cases and clears 68% of non-cases.

Predicted risks are too spread out: the calibration slope is 0.74, where 1 is perfect, so the highest risks are overstated and the lowest understated. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test finds no clear misfit (p = 0.237).
With every control at its typical value, the model estimates a 10.0% chance of CHD within 10 years. Move the controls to see how the estimate changes.

whatIf.note: Uses the full-data model, not the hold-out model. It shows what the model estimates from patterns in this data, not what would happen if a person changed.

takeaways.headline: 6 of 17 predictors show clear evidence of an association with CHD within 10 years. Discrimination is modest (AUC 0.70).

bullets.text: Prior stroke: 2.64 times the odds (95% CI 1.11 to 6.30).
Age: each 1 SD higher goes with 1.68 times the odds (95% CI 1.51 to 1.87).
Male (vs female): 1.63 times the odds (95% CI 1.34 to 1.99).

Modest discrimination. On the unseen test rows the model scores AUC 0.70 (5-fold cross-validation 0.73, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.78). At the chosen cut-off of 0.15 it catches 60% of cases and clears 68% of non-cases.
Current smoker and Cigarettes per day overlap, so read their odds ratios as a set (joint test, p < 0.001).
Hypertension, Systolic BP and Diastolic BP overlap, so read their odds ratios as a set (joint test, p < 0.001).
Diabetes and Glucose overlap, so read their odds ratios as a set (joint test, p < 0.001).

Using only the 3,658 complete rows changes whether there is clear evidence for Prior stroke and Total cholesterol, and moves the odds ratio for Prior stroke by 23%. The way gaps were filled matters for these results.
Removing the 42 most influential rows moves the odds ratio for Diabetes by 48%. That estimate rests on a few rows, so read it with caution. This is only a check: no row was removed from the model.

takeaways.nonSignificantNote: 11 predictors showed no clear evidence of an association: Education level: 2 vs 1, Education level: 3 vs 1, Education level: 4 vs 1, Current smoker and On BP medication and 6 more. They stay in the model. No clear evidence is not evidence that there is no effect.
caveats: These are associations in observational data, not proof that changing a factor changes the outcome.
Independence of rows is assumed, not tested.
The model learns from one dataset (Framingham Heart Study). Check it on other populations before relying on it.
The cut-off was tuned by cross-validation on the training rows; the hold-out test rows were used once.
